title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Portland, OR: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Portland: shipyard, bridge, rail and high-purity piping work, Part C code choice and where Oregon candidates test. Get a quote.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Portland, Oregon: Six Days to Get Ready for the CWI
html:
Portland, Oregon, is a working river port, and a surprising share of the steel welded here ends up in the water, over the water or carrying something across it. That makes the AWS Certified Welding Inspector credential a practical asset for welders, fitters and quality staff in the metro area. Atlantis NDT offers a six-day CWI exam-preparation course that Portland candidates either study online at their own pace or, when an employer wants several people ready at once, take as a six-day block at the employer's site. The examination and the certificate both belong to the American Welding Society: AWS sets the questions, runs the test and decides who becomes a CWI. Atlantis gets candidates ready and certifies no one. For a scoped proposal, request a Portland CWI prep quote; each of the six days is broken down on the national AWS CWI course page.

A port city that welds on the water

The Willamette River brings deep-draft ships into a harbor with terminals for containers, autos, liquid bulk, grain and mineral bulk, according to the Port of Portland. Downriver from downtown, the Swan Island industrial area holds Vigor's shipyard, with large floating dry docks that take commercial, government and Navy vessels for repair and new construction. Ship repair is weld-intensive in a way few other industries match: plate inserts, frame and stiffener renewals, piping replacement and hull penetrations, much of it done against a dry-dock schedule that rarely slips in the inspector's favor.

Ship work is usually governed by classification society rules or Navy technical requirements rather than the codes AWS offers for Part C. That surprises some candidates. The CWI is still valued in yards because the skills it tests travel: reading a procedure, confirming a welder is qualified for the position and thickness, measuring fillet size and profile, recognizing undercut, overlap and cracking, and writing a defensible record. Yard inspectors typically choose a Part C book that matches where they expect their careers to go, which for many is AWS D1.1 or the ASME option.

Along the Willamette in Northwest Portland, the fuel tank farms known as the Critical Energy Infrastructure Hub add storage tank, terminal piping and dock structure work. Tank repairs, nozzle additions and piping tie-ins on that kind of equipment are welded to qualified procedures, and contractors need inspectors who can check them before the NDT crew arrives.

Bridges on two rivers, and why D1.5 matters here

Portland is a bridge city, with crossings over the Willamette downtown and the Columbia to the north. The largest program on the horizon is the Interstate Bridge Replacement on I-5 between Portland and Vancouver, Washington. Steel bridge members are fabricated to AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, which state transportation departments call up in their contracts. D1.5 is stricter than the building code in several places that matter on the shop floor, including welder and procedure qualification and the extra controls on fracture-critical members.

For a candidate at a bridge fabricator, that points toward choosing AWS D1.5 for Part C. AWS listed the 2020 edition, including its Clause 12 on fracture-critical members, on its CWI page in November 2026. Inspectors who split time between bridge and building steel sometimes prefer AWS D1.1 because it covers more of their week; the two codes share structure, so learning one makes the other easier to navigate.

Clean rooms and high-purity piping west of the city

In the western suburbs, Intel's Hillsboro campus and the suppliers around it build ultra-high-purity gas and chemical systems from orbital-welded stainless tubing. The welds are small, the acceptance criteria are tight and discoloration or incomplete penetration on the inside surface can reject a joint. Much of that piping falls under ASME B31.3, including its high-purity provisions, with procedures and welders qualified under ASME Section IX. Quality staff in that world often pick the ASME option for Part C, which AWS describes as Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3. Our pages on ASME B31.3 and ASME Section IX explain both documents in plain language.

Rail cars and the D15.1 option

Railcar building along the Willamette and Columbia gives Portland a Part C choice that most cities never think about: AWS D15.1, the Railroad Welding Specification for Cars and Locomotives, which AWS listed in its 2019 edition. A quality inspector at a car builder or repair shop who works to D15.1 every day may find it the most natural book to sit, because familiarity with the code's layout is worth more on an open-book timed test than general welding knowledge. Candidates who expect to leave rail work should weigh that against the broader recognition of D1.1.

Oregon's boiler code and where the CWI fits

Boilers and pressure vessels in Oregon come under the state Building Codes Division. Its Boiler and Pressure Vessel Specialty Code, in the 2024 edition, adopts the 2023 National Board Inspection Code, the 2023 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, and ASME B31.1 and B31.3 with Oregon amendments. State rules set inspection frequencies; for example, power boilers are inspected every year. A CWI does not stand in for the jurisdictional or authorized inspector on that equipment, but a CWI on a repair contractor's staff is often the person who makes sure the welding behind a repair is documented well enough for that inspector to accept.

Working both sides of the Columbia

Crews based in Portland routinely work in Vancouver and the rest of southwest Washington. Crossing the river means a different state, a different transportation department and different building departments, and sometimes different contract language about who may inspect welding. The CWI is useful precisely because it is a personal AWS credential recognized on both sides of the river; it travels with the inspector, unlike a company-specific qualification. If your work routinely crosses the state line, note it when you scope training with us so the code-reading practice reflects both sets of projects.

Where Portland candidates take Parts A, B and C

AWS splits delivery. Fundamentals (Part A) and Code Application (Part C) are computer-based and taken at Prometric test centers; AWS says Prometric runs more than 450 such centers worldwide, more than 100 of them in the United States. Once AWS sends your confirmation letter, the eligibility code in it lets you book with Prometric, and the Portland metro candidate can usually find a center without long travel.

The practical (Part B) is held at AWS seminar and examination sites, normally the weekend after an AWS seminar at the same place. On the CWI training location list we checked on aws.org in November 2026, there was no Oregon or Washington city. The nearest listed location to Portland was Sacramento, California. That list changes, so look at the AWS Seminar and Exam Schedule before you commit, and assume you will travel for Part B. On the day, AWS wants photo identification, meaning a current driver's license or passport, plus your printed confirmation letter, and its application cutoff for the practical falls weeks before the exam date.

Learning the trade at PCC Rock Creek and through the pipe trades

Portland Community College has taught welding for about half a century. Its Welding Technology program is based at the Rock Creek Campus, where the college opened a renovated 10,000-square-foot welding shop with 58 booths in 2021. The program offers an Associate of Applied Science in Welding Technology and uses an open-entry, open-exit format that lets students work toward a certificate or degree at their own pace. Graduates head into fabrication, construction and the pipe trades; the college's own coverage mentions students aiming for the pipefitters' union, UA Local 290.

For a future CWI, the associate degree matters on the eligibility table. AWS lists two years of welding-related work experience for a candidate holding an associate degree or higher in welding or engineering technology, engineering or physical science, compared with five years for a high school diploma. AWS judges what counts, so keep transcripts and an honest record of your welding jobs, with dates and supervisors who can confirm them.

The Greater Oregon Section of AWS

AWS's section directory places Oregon in District 19 and lists a Greater Oregon Section, alongside Alaska, Alberta, British Columbia, Inland Empire, Puget Sound Olympic and Spokane. Local sections hold technical meetings, run student and scholarship events and connect working inspectors with people entering the field. Section membership is not a certification step, but it is one of the easier ways for a Portland welder to meet the CWIs and fabrication managers who can describe what the job looks like day to day. Contact details and meeting calendars are on aws.org.

Online study or an on-site week: choosing the format

Atlantis has no classroom or office in Oregon. Its offices are in Houston and Hyderabad, and the course reaches Portland in two forms.

Self-paced online. The individual candidate gets a study plan built on the six course days, course materials, original practice questions, timed mock papers and a channel for questions to an instructor. Nothing is scheduled. That fits dry-dock crews whose hours swing with each vessel, bridge fabrication staff working overtime ahead of a delivery and anyone fitting study around family and shifts.

Six days on your premises. A shipyard subcontractor, bridge fabricator or high-purity piping contractor can host the whole six-day block in its own shop for a crew. Practical exercises then use the company's gauges and real welds from its production, and the code day works in the book the shop builds to. AWS still treats each candidate as an individual applicant who meets the eligibility and vision requirements and pays AWS directly.

What the six-day outline covers

  1. Fundamentals I. Welding processes and terminology to AWS A3.0, joint design and weld symbols to AWS A2.4.
  2. Fundamentals II. The metallurgy an inspector actually uses; tensile, bend, hardness and impact tests; how porosity, slag, lack of fusion and cracks form; what each NDT method can find; safety; and the ethics of signing an inspection record.
  3. Practical. Gauging weld size and profile, applying procedure and qualification records, accepting against supplied criteria; on-site groups practise with their own tools and samples.
  4. Code application. Finding definitions, tables and acceptance clauses quickly in the book you chose.
  5. Timed practice. Mock papers for all three parts under time pressure, then review of each wrong answer.
  6. Readiness. Weak-topic review, exam-day pacing and a checklist for the AWS application.

Every practice question is written by Atlantis against the topic areas AWS publishes; none comes from a real AWS paper. The national CWI course page gives the detail for each day.

Where Portland candidates usually need the most work

Each local industry sends people to CWI preparation with a different strength and a different blind spot, and knowing yours early is the best use of the first study weeks.

  • Shipyard welders and fitters tend to handle gauges and visual judgment well, so Part B feels familiar. The harder part is Part A breadth: metallurgy, heat treatment, destructive test interpretation and welding processes the yard rarely uses.
  • Bridge fabrication staff often know their shop's D1.5 provisions by heart but have never been asked to explain hydrogen cracking or calculate a weld metal volume against a clock.
  • High-purity piping quality staff are strong on documentation and traceability, yet many have spent little time on structural fillet welds, weld symbols with multiple reference lines or groove weld nomenclature.
  • Railcar inspectors usually need extra time on the parts of Part A that sit outside sheet and plate work, such as pipe joint terminology and the ASME qualification concepts that appear in general questions.

The timed practice papers on day five show which of these gaps is yours, and day six is spent closing it.

Exam essentials for Oregon candidates

ItemWhat AWS published (checked November 2026)
Governing standardAWS QC1:2016-AMD1, Specification for AWS Certification of Welding Inspectors
Part A, Fundamentals150 questions, computer-based at Prometric
Part B, PracticalHands-on activities with AWS equipment and 46 questions, at AWS sites
Part C, Code ApplicationOpen book, about 50 to 65 questions on your chosen code, computer-based at Prometric
Minimum score72 percent on each part
VisionJaeger J2 or better at no less than 12 inches, glasses allowed, plus a color perception check, recorded on the AWS form
Certificate lifeNine years, with renewals at years three and six
FeesSet by AWS and posted on aws.org; see the CWI exam spending planner

More background: what the CWI requires and what it does for a career and how results break down across Parts A, B and C.

Welding inspection and NDT in the Portland market

Shipyards, bridge fabricators and tank owners in Portland ask for ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant testing as well as visual weld inspection. Those NDT methods are performed by technicians whom their employer certifies under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, a separate route from the CWI. Many Portland inspectors combine the two. Atlantis delivers SNT-TC-1A-based training for the area, covered on the NDT training in Portland page, and the VT Level 1 course is a natural companion to CWI study. Local inspection services are described on visual testing in Portland and magnetic particle testing in Portland.

When you write to us, say how many people the course is for, give each candidate's education and years of welding work in rough terms, name the Part C code each intends to sit, and for on-site delivery tell us where the shop or yard is and which weeks avoid a dry-dock rush or a delivery deadline. The Portland CWI course enquiry reaches the training desk, which answers within one business day.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a CWI training center in Portland?
faq.a: No. Atlantis offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. Portland candidates study the six-day course online, or an employer books the six days at its own shop or yard for a group. The outline is on the AWS CWI exam prep page.

faq.q: Where would a Portland candidate sit the CWI practical?
faq.a: AWS holds Part B at its seminar and examination sites. When we checked aws.org in November 2026, no Oregon or Washington city was on its CWI location list, and Sacramento was the nearest. Parts A and C are computer-based at Prometric centers, which are easier to find locally.

faq.q: Which Part C code suits a bridge fabricator in Portland?
faq.a: Bridge steel inspectors in Portland mostly sit D1.5, since the transportation departments on both sides of the Columbia write it into their contracts. People who also cover building steel sometimes prefer D1.1.

faq.q: Is there a Part C option for railcar work?
faq.a: Yes. AWS lists D15.1, the Railroad Welding Specification for Cars and Locomotives, among the Part C options. It suits inspectors who already work to it at car builders or repair shops.

faq.q: I work in a shipyard. Is the CWI still relevant if ship work follows class or Navy rules?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Those rules are not Part C options, but the skills the CWI tests, such as procedure review, welder qualification checks and visual acceptance, carry straight into yard work. Most yard candidates choose D1.1 or the ASME option.

faq.q: How does a PCC welding degree affect CWI eligibility?
faq.a: AWS lists two years of welding-related experience for candidates with an associate degree or higher in welding or engineering technology, engineering or physical science, while a diploma-only applicant needs five. The final call on qualifying work rests with AWS.
AWS administers the examination and issues the certification. Atlantis prepares candidates and does not certify anyone, set the exam or see results.

faq.q: Is there an AWS section for Portland?
faq.a: The AWS directory lists a Greater Oregon Section in District 19. Meeting details are on aws.org.

faq.q: Can a Portland employer have the course delivered at its facility?
faq.a: Yes. The six days can run at your site for a group, with practice on your own gauges and welds. Request a quote.

faq.q: Should I add NDT training to the CWI?
faq.a: Many Portland inspectors do. NDT methods such as UT, MT and PT are certified by the employer under ASNT SNT-TC-1A. See NDT training in Portland.
